newsitem.title: USA: Seattle football stadium alive despite setback.
newsitem.headline: Seattle football stadium alive despite setback.

text.p: The Washington state Senate should quickly revive Legislation that would finance a proposed Seahawk football stadium in Seattle was dealt a setback but should be revived quickly in the state Senate, one of its sponsors said Tuesday.

"We just lost some yards," said Democratic state Sen. Jeanne Kohl, who sits on the Senate Ways and Means Committee. "But we'll have other opportunities to move the ball down the field to the goal line."
Late Monday, the committee voted 18-3 to reject a financing plan for the proposed $402 million stadium.

Multibillionaire investor Paul Allen, the Microsoft Corp. co-founder who last year negotiated an exclusive option to buy the Seattle Seahawks and keep the team in Seattle, said the vote was "extremely disappointing."
In a statement, Allen threatened to drop his option to purchase the team if "acceptable" legislation was not enacted by April 3 to put the stadium financing package on a June ballot.
Allen has paid $20 million for his option to buy the Seahawks, which expires in July, but he has demanded public stadium financing and a public vote before he will complete the deal.
"There appears to be some misunderstanding that the option would be executed without a legislatively approved funding mechanism and without the voters' approval," Allen said.
"Let me be clear. I do not intent to proceed with the purchase option if the legislature and the voters do not approve a reasonable funding plan."

Kohl said Tuesday that state Senate leadership could revive the financing package by bringing the measure directly to the floor. If that fails, Kohl said a House version of the bill could be advanced to the Senate.
"The bill is not dead in the Senate," Kohl said.
Democractic Gov. Gary Locke was disappointed by the vote but has not given up hope, an aide said.
"We're going to continue working with the Legislature at this point and see what alternatives we have. Nothing is entirely dead around here," said Marty Brown, a lobbyist for Locke.
